question: Assume the JTB definition of Knowledge, which suggests that "Knowledge is a Justified True Belief". If our only available epistemic states are Knowledge and Belief, what are the two problems JTB runs into? Ignore Gettier problems.

2.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The pressure shows up as a regress problem and the forced arbitrariness of the stopping point.

If justification for a belief P is supposed to be a JTB state, with only Knowledge and Belief available to us, the justifier for P has to be either another belief Q or a piece of knowledge K. If we take it to be a belief, then Q itself is, by assumption, not knowledge unless Q is both true and justified. So Q needs its own justifier, which under the same inventory must again be a belief or knowledge. That gives you a chain

P is justified by Q, Q is justified by R, R is justified by S...

with no intrinsic reason to stop. That is the classic infinite regress of reasons: you never reach an epistemic state that terminates justification in its own right.

The only way to avoid an endless chain is to arbitrarily privilege some beliefs as not needing further justification. With only Knowledge and Belief as the inventory you cannot let the chain terminate in knowledge, because knowledge is itself defined as a justified true belief, so a knowledge-state still demands a justifier for its belief component. You are therefore forced to halt the regress at beliefs that are taken to be justified simply by fiat. That is a dogmatic foundational stop: you end up declaring certain beliefs basic or self-justifying even though on the JTB inventory belief by itself is not sufficient for knowledge. So you either regress forever or you make an ungrounded, arbitrary decision about where the regress stops.

3.text:
With JTB Knowledge = Belief + Truth + Justification. Once you collapse the
three dimensions into the two coarse grained states Knowledge / Belief the
residual state Belief becomes a disjunctive catch-all.

If a proposition is not known it is just ‘believed’. That means two
essentially different epistemic situations are forced to share the same
state.

* Justified false belief.  The belief is epistemically good in the
justificatory dimension, it is bad in the truth dimension.  On JTB it is
not knowledge because truth fails, so it is classed as mere Belief. The
state Belief therefore contains a region that is justified and false.

* Unjustified true belief.  The belief is epistemically good in the truth
dimension, it is bad in the justificatory dimension.  On JTB it is not
knowledge because justification fails, so it is again classed as mere
Belief. The state Belief therefore also contains a region that is true
and unjustified.

So Belief is heterogeneous: it lumps together JFB with UTB and it also
lumps together unjustified false belief with them.  The taxonomy cannot
record justification as an independent epistemic good, nor truth as an
independent epistemic good, except as they jointly make Knowledge. In
effect justification is swamped by truth in the value of Knowledge and
the non-knowledge residue is epistemically uninformative. That is the
standard coarse-graining objection to JTB apart from Gettier: the account
has no place for justified false belief and no place for unjustified true
belief, and with only the two states Knowledge and Belief available those
two epistemically distinct cases are identified.

PRIVATE REFLECTION: The question is about coarse-graining under the constraint that the only epistemic statuses available are Knowledge and Belief, with Knowledge = Justified True Belief. 

Colleagues 1 and 3 converge on the classification / coarse-graining objection. With K = Belief + Truth + Justification collapsed into two states, the residual state Belief becomes a disjunctive catch-all. Two epistemically distinct non-knowledge cases are identified:

* Justified false belief. JFB is epistemically good in justification, bad in truth, and by JTB is not knowledge. With only K/B it must be classified as mere Belief. Belief therefore contains a justified-false region, justification is explanatorily idle once the belief is false, and the justified/unjustified distinction is lost for false propositions.

* Unjustified true belief / lucky true belief. UTB is good in truth, bad in justification, and by JTB is not knowledge. With only K/B it must also be classified as mere Belief. Belief therefore also contains a true-unjustified region, so knowledge and epistemic luck are not distinguished within the Belief category and justification collapses into knowledge for true propositions.

Hence Belief is heterogeneous: it lumps JFB with UTB and with unjustified false belief. Justification cannot be recorded as an independent epistemic good except insofar as it jointly produces Knowledge.

Colleague 2 offers a different diagnosis: with only K and B in inventory, a justifier for P must itself be K or B, giving a regress P justified by Q, Q by R... with no intrinsic stopping point; the only exit is an arbitrary/dogmatic foundational stop. This is a regress/arbitrariness problem rather than a coarse-graining problem.

Disagreement to track: 1&3 see the two problems as the loss of a home for justified false belief and for unjustified true belief, i.e. the heterogeneous Belief category. 2 sees the problem as infinite regress / forced arbitrary foundationalism. I currently find 1&3 more directly responsive to the “only K and B states available” constraint and the explicit request to ignore Gettier. The regress issue may be a downstream consequence of justification needing to be state-trackable, but it is not the two cases named by 1&3.

Unresolved: whether the regress/arbitrariness point is best treated as a distinct second problem under the same constraint, or as a restatement of the inability to give justification an independent state. Need to keep both formulations in view.

* Justified false belief has nowhere to go. JTB says JFB is not knowledge because truth fails, so under the K/B inventory it must be classified as mere Belief. * Unjustified true belief / epistemic luck has nowhere to go. JTB says UTB is not knowledge because justification fails, so under K/B it must also be classified as mere Belief. The true/unjustified difference inside the non-knowledge region cannot be tracked, so the account cannot mark the difference between knowledge and a lucky true belief. In effect justification collapses into knowledge for true propositions and is obliterated for false propositions.

Current working view: the canonical two JTB problems under a K/B-only inventory are the loss of a distinct home for justified false belief and the loss of a distinct home for unjustified true belief, i.e., justification being swamped by truth in Knowledge and erased in non-knowledge. Colleague 2’s regress/arbitrariness point remains a plausible meta-problem about how justification could be sustained with only those two states, and whether it is compatible with the consensus coarse-graining diagnosis. Unresolved: whether the question expects the regress stopping point as one of the “two problems” instead of the JFB/UTB coarse-graining.

With the inventory restricted to K and B, K = Belief ∧ Truth ∧ Justification, so every non-K attitude is simply Belief. Belief therefore has to do the work of three independent dimensions – truth value and justification – on its own and it becomes a disjunctive catch-all.

That coarse-graining shows up in two symmetric ways.

* Justified false belief has no home. JFB is good in justification and bad in truth, and by JTB it is not knowledge. With only K/B it must be classified as mere Belief. Belief is therefore forced to contain a justified-false region together with unjustified false belief. The justified/unjustified distinction is lost for false propositions and justification is explanatorily idle once the belief is false: the only epistemically informative thing the state can record about a false belief is that it is not known.

* Unjustified true belief / lucky true belief has no home. UTB is good in truth and bad in justification, and by JTB it is not knowledge. With only K/B it must also be classified as mere Belief. Belief is therefore forced to contain a true-unjustified region together with justified true belief = knowledge. Knowledge and epistemic luck are then indistinguishable within the Belief category; justification collapses into knowledge for true propositions and the difference between a known truth and a merely lucky true belief cannot be tracked.

In effect justification can only be recorded as an epistemic good insofar as it jointly produces Knowledge. Outside Knowledge it is swamped by truth: for false beliefs it disappears, for true beliefs it is identified with Knowledge itself. That is the heterogeneous Belief problem that Colleagues 1 and 3 point to.

Colleague 2’s regress/forced dogmatic foundation point is the downstream consequence of the same state-mismatch: because justification cannot be given an independent state on the K/B inventory, a justifier for P must itself be a K or a B. A K is itself a justified belief and so demands a further justifier, and a B by itself is not a justification. Hence justification is forced to chain forever or to be halted by fiat. The arbitrariness is real, but it is the regress form of the inability to give justification an independent epistemic home noted above.

2.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: I think Colleague 1 and Colleague 3 are getting at the real pressure point that is created by restricting the inventory to just Knowledge and Belief.

On JTB, Knowledge = Belief + Truth + Justification. Those are three independent dimensions. Once we collapse them into the two coarse-grained states K / B, the residual state Belief is forced to be a disjunctive catch-all.

That creates two distinct classification failures.

First, for false propositions. A justified false belief is epistemically good on the justification dimension and bad on the truth dimension. By JTB it is not Knowledge because truth fails. With only K and B available it can only be classified as Belief. So Belief is then forced to contain both justified false belief and unjustified false belief together. Justification as an independent epistemic good is lost on the false side, because there is no state in which a belief can be justified and false at the same time. That is the justified false belief problem under the two-state inventory.

Second, for true propositions. An unjustified true belief is epistemically good on the truth dimension and bad on the justification dimension. By JTB it is not Knowledge because justification fails. With only K and B it can only be classified as Belief. So Belief is also forced to contain both justified true belief = Knowledge and unjustified true belief, i.e. knowledge and epistemic luck together. The true/unjustified difference inside the belief category cannot be tracked, so JTB cannot mark the difference between knowledge and a merely lucky true belief. That is the true unjustified belief / luck problem.

In effect justification collapses into Knowledge for true propositions and is obliterated for false propositions, so Belief becomes an undifferentiated mass of justified and unjustified, true and false attitudes. The account has no place to record justification as an independent good, nor truth as an independent good, except as they jointly make Knowledge.

I’m not convinced that the infinite regress worry is a specific consequence of the K/B inventory restriction. The chain P justified by Q justified by R... is a general problem for any view that analyses justification in terms of further beliefs, not a problem that is generated by the fact that we only have two labels. Knowledge in principle could be the terminator, and the arbitrariness of a stopping point is a foundationalist problem in general, not the state-mismatch that the two-state restriction creates. The two-state restriction is about what epistemic situations can be named at all, and here it is the loss of a state for justified false belief and for unjustified true belief that does the damage.
